Title: Transformers with RL or SFT Provably Learn Sparse Boolean Functions, But Differently
Authors: Bochen Lyu, Yiyang Jia, Xiaohao Cai, Zhanxing Zhu
Date: Sat Nov 22 00:38:43 2025

Transformers can acquire Chain-of-Thought (CoT) capabilities to solve complex reasoning tasks through fine-tuning. Reinforcement learning (RL) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) are two primary approaches to this end, yet their underlying mechanisms and differences remain theoretically unclear. In this work, we examine these aspects specifically for learning $k$-sparse Boolean functions with a one-layer transformer and intermediate supervision that is akin to CoT. In particular, we consider $k$-sparse Boolean functions that can be recursively decomposed into fixed 2-sparse Boolean functions. We analyze the learning dynamics of fine-tuning the transformer via either RL or SFT with CoT to identify sufficient conditions for it to provably learn these functions. We verify that these conditions hold for three basic examples, including $k$-PARITY, $k$-AND, and $k$-OR, thus demonstrating the learnability of both approaches. Notably, we reveal that RL and SFT exhibit distinct learning behaviors: RL learns the whole CoT chain simultaneously, whereas SFT learns the CoT chain step-by-step. Overall, our findings provide theoretical insights into the underlying mechanisms of RL and SFT as well as how they differ in triggering the CoT capabilities of transformers.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Title: Equivalence of Context and Parameter Updates in Modern Transformer Blocks
Authors: Adrian Goldwaser, Michael Munn, Javier Gonzalvo, Benoit Dherin
Date: Sat Nov 22 01:17:15 2025

Recent research has established that the impact of context in a vanilla transformer can be represented implicitly by forming a token-dependent, rank-1 patch to its MLP weights. This work extends that foundational theory to the diverse architectures of modern Large Language Models. We first demonstrate a precise, analytical solution for a Gemma-style transformer block, proving that the entire effect of a context can be perfectly mapped to rank-1 patches on its MLP weight matrices and a patch to the RMSNorm scale. We then generalize this result, providing a constructive proof and algorithm for multi-layer models. To unify these findings, we introduce a general framework centered on two core properties: input controllability and output controllability. We prove that a perfect implicit weight patch is possible for any MLP block where the inner function is input-controllable and the outer function is output-controllable. This provides a simpler and more powerful lens for understanding how transformer models transmute prompts into effective weights. This setup generalizes to a wide range of modern LLM architectures including gating, pre-/post-norm, mixture of experts and sequential/parallel transformer blocks.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Title: No Free Lunch in Language Model Bias Mitigation? Targeted Bias Reduction Can Exacerbate Unmitigated LLM Biases
Authors: Shireen Chand, Faith Baca, Emilio Ferrara
Date: Sun Nov 23 22:21:18 2025

Large Language Models (LLMs) inherit societal biases from their training data, potentially leading to harmful or unfair outputs. While various techniques aim to mitigate these biases, their effects are often evaluated only along the dimension of the bias being targeted. This work investigates the cross-category consequences of targeted bias mitigation. We study four bias mitigation techniques applied across ten models from seven model families, and we explore racial, religious, profession- and gender-related biases. We measure the impact of debiasing on model coherence and stereotypical preference using the StereoSet benchmark. Our results consistently show that while targeted mitigation can sometimes reduce bias in the intended dimension, it frequently leads to unintended and often negative consequences in others, such as increasing model bias and decreasing general coherence. These findings underscore the critical need for robust, multi-dimensional evaluation tools when examining and developing bias mitigation strategies to avoid inadvertently shifting or worsening bias along untargeted axes.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Title: An Online Fragmentation-Aware GPU Scheduler for Multi-Tenant MIG-based Clouds
Authors: Marco Zambianco, Lorenzo Fasol, Roberto Doriguzzi-Corin
Date: Mon Nov 24 09:10:35 2025

The explosive growth of AI applications has created unprecedented demand for GPU resources. Cloud providers meet this demand through GPU-as-a-Service platforms that offer rentable GPU resources for running AI workloads. In this context, the sharing of GPU resources between different tenants is essential to maximize the number of scheduled workloads. Among the various GPU sharing technologies, NVIDIA's Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) stands out by partitioning GPUs at hardware level into isolated slices with dedicated compute and memory, ensuring strong tenant isolation, preventing resource contention, and enhancing security. Despite these advantages, MIG's fixed partitioning introduces scheduling rigidity, leading to severe GPU fragmentation in multi-tenant environments, where workloads are continuously deployed and terminated. Fragmentation leaves GPUs underutilized, limiting the number of workloads that can be accommodated. To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel scheduling framework for MIG-based clouds that maximizes workload acceptance while mitigating fragmentation in an online, workload-agnostic setting. We introduce a fragmentation metric to quantify resource inefficiency and guide allocation decisions. Building on this metric, our greedy scheduling algorithm selects GPUs and MIG slices that minimize fragmentation growth for each incoming workload. We evaluate our approach against multiple baseline strategies under diverse workload distributions. Results demonstrate that our method consistently achieves higher workload acceptance rates, leading to an average 10% increase in the number of scheduled workloads in heavy load conditions, while using approximately the same number of GPUs as the benchmark methods.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Equivalence of Context and Parameter Updates in Modern Transformer Blocks

Adrian Goldwaser, Michael Munn, Javier Gonzalvo, Benoit Dherin

arXiv 2025

Read Paper Bookmark

## TL;DR

This paper proves that the effect of a prompt (context) in modern Large Language Models can be mathematically mapped to precise, rank-1 parameter updates—or "patches"—to the model's weights. By introducing a unified framework of "input and output controllability," the authors demonstrate that in-context learning can be viewed as a dynamic form of implicit fine-tuning across diverse modern architectures like Gemma, Llama, and Mistral.

## What Problem Does This Paper Address?

In-context learning (ICL) is the remarkable ability of LLMs to learn new tasks on the fly purely from the prompt, without any explicit updates to their weights. Recent theoretical work showed that for a vanilla transformer, this contextual influence is mathematically equivalent to temporary rank-1 patches applied to the MLP weights and biases.

However, modern high-performance LLMs have evolved significantly. They use gated MLPs (like SwiGLU and GeGLU), substitute LayerNorm with RMSNorm, implement pre-normalization schemes, and completely eliminate biases. Because previous proofs relied heavily on biases to absorb the impact of residual connections, a major gap remained: Does this "context-as-weight-updates" equivalence still hold for modern, bias-free architectures?

## Methods

The authors bridge this gap through a mix of constructive proofs, algorithmic design, and architectural generalization:

  * Gemma Block Analytical Solution: The authors derive exact mathematical updates for a Gemma-style block, demonstrating that the entire context can be absorbed into rank-1 patches on the gating and upside weight matrices ($W_{\text{gate}}$, $W_{\text{up}}$), alongside an element-wise patch to the RMSNorm scaling vector ($m$).
  * Multi-Layer Induction: They extend this single-block proof to deep networks using a layer-by-layer sequential algorithm (Algorithm 1). This algorithm runs a forward pass with full context to record target activations, then computes updates inductively to prevent numerical error accumulation.
  * Controllability Framework: To generalize beyond Gemma, they introduce a unified framework based on two core properties:
  * Input Controllability: The ability of an inner function to counteract input shifts via weight updates.
  * Output Controllability: The ability of an outer function to absorb residual shifts at the output boundary.
  * Numerically Stable Update: To handle lower-precision datatypes (`bfloat16`) used in production, they derive an analytical inversion of RMSNorm. This shifts the mathematical burden of the update from the global scaling vector to the $W_{\text{down}}$ weight matrix, mitigating division-by-zero issues.
Image: Gemma MLP block diagram showing the components targeted for parameter updates.Expand

Figure 1. Gemma MLP block diagram. m is part of the second RMS normalization (RMSNorm2) but stated separately to match the equations. ⊗denotes elementwise multiplication of vectors.

## Datasets

Rather than training on standard datasets, the authors evaluate their mathematical equivalence empirically using pre-trained models (Gemma 3 1B/4B and Falcon 7B) across several distinct prompts:

  * Textual Contexts: Creative writing tasks (e.g., "Write a single-sentence weather forecast for Mars, from the perspective of a slightly annoyed robot"), constrained generation, analogies, and poetry.
  * Multimodal Contexts: Image-based prompts to validate the framework on vision-language inputs.

## Key Insights and Ideas

  * Separation of Concerns: The framework elegantly splits the problem: rank-1 updates to the input weights counteract changes in the normalized input vector (input controllability), while updates to the output scale vector perfectly absorb differences from the pre-normalization residual path (output controllability).
  * The Necessity of the Scaling Vector: The authors prove a striking negative result: output controllability fails if an architecture uses RMS post-normalization without a trainable scaling vector $m$. Without $m$, the output is trapped on an $L_2$ sphere, making it geometrically impossible to stretch and absorb arbitrary contextual shifts.
  * Connection to Gradient Descent: These implicit patches are not just algebraic parlor tricks. The authors show they can be derived exactly as gradient descent steps on a specific "trace-loss" meta-objective, providing a mechanistic link between in-context learning and standard backpropagation.
Image: Multi-layer equivalence diagram showing how context is stripped and replaced with updated parameters layer-by-layer.Expand

Extracted figure from page 4 of Equivalence of Context and Parameter Updates in Modern Transformer Blocks

## Key Results

  * Perfect Equivalence in FP32: In `float32` precision, the patched model operating without any context perfectly replicates the next-token logit distributions and token generation of the original model with context.
  * 100% Match in Lower Precision: In `bfloat16`, the naive update method degrades to an 87.5% token match due to numerical instability from dividing by near-zero activations. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# An Online Fragmentation-Aware GPU Scheduler for Multi-Tenant MIG-based Clouds

Is GPU fragmentation killing your cloud's performance? This paper has the fix.

Published 11/25/2025 by Marco Zambianco, Lorenzo Fasol, Roberto Doriguzzi Corin

## Overview

  * GPUs are expensive resources, so cloud providers split them into smaller pieces using Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) technology to serve multiple customers simultaneously
  * When jobs finish and leave the GPU, fragmentation occurs—usable space becomes scattered across the GPU in ways that make it hard to fit new jobs
  * This paper introduces a scheduling algorithm that considers fragmentation when deciding which jobs to run, reducing wasted GPU capacity
  * The algorithm works online, making decisions in real-time without knowing future job arrivals
  * Testing shows the approach improves GPU utilization compared to existing methods

## Plain English Explanation

Think of a GPU as a parking lot. When you divide it into smaller spaces for different customers, you can fit more cars. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
